newsitem.title: TURKEY: Main players in Turkey government crisis.
newsitem.headline: Main players in Turkey government crisis.

text.p: Here are snap shots of the main players in the scramble to find a new Turkish government. Talks between leaders began on Thursday, a day after the resignation of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan:

-- Suleyman Demirel: A veteran conservative. Demirel was prime minister seven times in a political career spanning four decades that saw him toppled twice from the top post by the military. He became president in 1993 when incumbent Turgut Ozal died.
Demirel, whose post is largely symbolic, must choose from among party leaders one who is capable of forming a government within the finely-balanced national assembly of 550 MPs.

-- Necmettin Erbakan: Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, Erbakan quit after a public tussle with the staunchly secularist army over an alleged increase in religious activism since he came to power a year ago.

Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party is the biggest group in parliament with 156 seats. He is looking to revamp his coalition with the pro-Western True Path Party under the premiership of True Path's leader, Tansu Ciller.

-- Tansu Ciller: A U.S.-educated economist. She became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993 and shocked many last June by dragging her party into a coalition with the Islamists. An astute political tactician, she persuaded Erbakan to resign and try to transfer power to her to defuse tension with the army.
Ciller's party has 116 MPs and has been beset by defections among those disillusioned with the pro-Islamic alliance.

-- Mesut Yilmaz: Leader of the second largest party with 129 MPs. Precedent dictates that the president offer Yilmaz the first chance to form a government after Erbakan's resignation but there are no certainties.

Yilmaz's free-market Motherland Party has almost identical policies to Ciller's grouping, although a bitter personal rivalry ruined a short-lived coalition between the pair last June and makes another similar alliance unlikely.
Yilmaz, slow-spoken and earnest, has been prime minister briefly twice but secularist commentators complain he lacks the punch needed to tackle the Islamists.
-- Muhsin Yazicioglu: Former leader of the ultra-right "Grey Wolves" movement, notorious for street fighting with left-wingers in the 1970s.

Yazicioglu and his seven MPs could hold the balance in a vote of confidence in any new government. He has announced he would support the effort to resurrect Erbakan's coalition under Ciller's leadership.

-- Deniz Baykal: The secularist media has promoted Baykal, cultured and charismatic, as the man to halt the Islamists in the long term. His left-wing Republican Peoples' Party was founded in the 1920s by secularist hero Kemal Ataturk.

-- Bulent Ecevit: As prime minister in 1974, Ecevit gained much popularity for ordering Turkish troops to invade Cyprus following a Greek Cypriot coup. His Democratic Left Party is the larger of the left-wing parties and has 67 MPs.
-- Husamettin Cindoruk: His party's seven MPs are defectors from Ciller's faction who were upset at her alliance with the Islamists.
